slides.authors: Ann Meier, Claire Kamp Dush, Alexandra VanBergen, Sierra Clark, and 2 others
slides.snippet: This project assessed parental stress in 2020 and 2021 during a period of racial trauma marked by high-profile, race-motivated murders of people of color. Framing inclusion: discursive logics of entitlement in immigrant social rights advocacy
slides.snippet: This article investigates how civil society organizations (CSOs) advocate for immigrant access to social assistance in politically charged environments. It explores whether the frame choices of CSOs are shaped by their relationships with government bodies and examines the implications of these narratives for representing a highly diverse group of non-citizens.

The stalled gender housework revolution in the United States
slides.snippet: Prior studies document a declining but persistent gender housework gap since the 1960s, with declines in women’s housework time far exceeding increases in men’s. slides.title: Narrations of non-motherhood: how context shapes what it means to be childless in the United States and Japan
slides.snippet: In our era of low fertility rates, much research has examined factors behind delayed childbearing and childlessness. While scholars emphasize the role of macro-level context in constraining reproductive decision-making, less attention has been paid to how context shapes what it means, subjectively, to remain childless today.

slides.authors: Irem Tuncer-Ebetürk, Jessica Kim, and Yasemin Nuhoğlu Soysal
slides.snippet: In the past three decades, the global diagnosis rate of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) has grown drastically. While existing sociological studies demonstrate the complexity of ADHD diagnoses and treatment in specific national contexts, their ability to explain ADHD’s global growth is limited.

slides.hook: Who has to prove they can do the job? White men are hired on assumed ability; Black men, Black women, and White women must match every requirement to get the same shot.

slides.title: Higher education expansion and attainment gaps in meritocratic beliefs
slides.snippet: Over the past decades, higher education has expanded dramatically worldwide, yet how this transformation shapes public beliefs in meritocracy remains underexplored. This study examines how the expansion of higher education has shaped public beliefs in meritocracy across thirty Western countries.

slides.title: Colonial legacy and contemporary civil violence: a global study from 1960 to 2018
slides.snippet: This study assesses whether the legacy of colonialism continues to influence patterns of civil violence in the contemporary era. A large and established quantitative literature attributes civil violence to low levels of economic development and limited political rights, but few quantitative studies consider whether colonial legacy plays an enduring role in such conflicts.

slides.hook: Asked about jobs, family, and faith, ordinary Americans kept slipping into conspiracy talk unprompted, one in ten of them. In the pandemic, most of the rise was people pushing back.

slides.authors: Niko Pyrhönen, Gwenaëlle Bauvois, Anton Berg, and Peter Holley

slides.title: Later life social interactions in community spaces
slides.authors: Maleah Fekete, Tianyao Qu, Brea L Perry, Siyun Peng, and Adam R Roth
slides.snippet: Daily social interactions provide access to key social resources, yet little research has examined how these interactions vary across geographic space—particularly in later life. Using ecological momentary assessment data from a state-representative study of older adults in Indiana, we examine how interactions with different partners vary across a continuum of municipality population density.

slides.hook: What teaches people to share power in democratic schools and collectives isn't a rulebook. Veteran members hold back their own influence and let slow, messy decisions play out, so newcomers learn to lead.
slides.title: Filling the collective-practice gap: pedagogies of participation in participatory-democratic organizations
Paving the way: redlining and contemporary transportation emissions in US cities
slides.authors: Rachel McKane and Patrick Trent Greiner
slides.snippet: We expand upon the structural human ecology tradition by recasting its classic drivers as historically racialized mechanisms operating within a system of racial capitalism. We draw on critical approaches to environmental justice to link multiscalar processes to material infrastructures, theorizing redlining and interstate-highway planning as coupled racial projects that organize the production of transportation emissions across urban space.

slides.hook: What do right-to-work laws cost workers beyond wages? Retirement and health coverage. Benefits eroded where the laws passed, and Indiana's would have held up better without one.
slides.title: For what benefit? State Right to Work laws and employer-provided retirement and health insurance benefits
Job precarity and earnings inequality in contemporary China
slides.snippet: Job precarity is a core mechanism of workplace inequality that underlies economic segmentation between organizational insiders and outsiders. Yet less is known about how institutional contexts affect dual employment arrangements that create differential rewards between long-term and short-term workers.

slides.hook: What builds expertise among Argentina's agroecology farmers isn't official training. It's discernment, weighing state advice against their own goals, keeping what fits and dropping what serves agribusiness.
slides.title: A work of discernment: the co-construction of environmental expertise among agroecology farmers
A work of discernment: the co-construction of environmental expertise among agroecology farmers
slides.snippet: Agroecology—a food production and consumption model that integrates ecological, social, and economic sustainability principles—underwent a period of significant growth in recent years in Argentina. Acquiring specialized knowledge about agroecology practices is a priority for farmers who pursue socio-environmental goals, but the process for building such expertise is not clearly laid out.

slides.hook: Environmental racism is often treated as recent. But in six US cities from 1880 to 1930, racialized neighborhoods already faced steadily rising industrial pollution, so it took root far earlier than thought.
slides.title: Environment and the racialization of space in US cities

slides.hook: Pay gaps are widest inside the best-paid groups, and here's why: already high earners are the ones who land in the top-paying firms and jobs, and that pull gets stronger the higher you go.
slides.title: The nonlinear nature of labor market sorting: explaining wage inequalities between and within sociodemographic groups
